title: YouTube subtitles and translation, even without captions · Titl
metaDesc: Free Chrome extension that adds subtitles and translation to almost any YouTube video, even with no captions. Runs Whisper on your own computer.
heroLead: Even videos with no captions at all. Titl listens to the video on your own computer a few seconds ahead, so each line appears right as it's spoken. Private, free and open source, in about 100 languages.
heroBrowsers: Chrome, Edge and Brave on macOS, Windows and Linux.
shotAlt: Titl showing Serbian subtitles with an English translation on a TEDx talk
shotCaption: Titl's own output on Tatjana Vojtehovski at TEDxZemun: Serbian on top, English translation below.
whyText: Most live-caption tools show each line after it's spoken, send your audio to the cloud, or only work when the video already has captions. Titl does the work on your own computer, prepares subtitles ahead of what you're watching, and works on almost any video.
f1a: Right on time: Titl quietly listens a few seconds ahead in a hidden tab, so each line appears as it's spoken.
f1b: Live streams work too, with subtitles a few seconds behind.
f1c: Keeps up when you skip, change speed, sit through ads or switch videos.
f2a: Audio never leaves your computer: speech is recognised right on your machine, not in the cloud.
f2b: No sign-up, no tracking, no ads.
f2c: Free and open source, so anyone can check what it does.
f3a: Translation into about 36 languages, done right on your computer by Chrome.
f3d: New: AI translation. A free AI model on your own computer reads whole sentences, not single lines. How to set it up
f3b: Original and translation together, or just the translation.
f3c: Blur the translation to practise listening: V or a click reveals it.
f4a: Uses one of the most accurate speech-recognition models available.
f4c: Serbian: always Latin or always Cyrillic, never a mix.
f5a: One small helper app downloads and sets up everything it needs.
f5b: Nothing to start by hand: click Start subtitles and it's ready.
f5c: Windows: download, double-click, done. Updates take one click.
f6a: Subtitles in normal and fullscreen, never over YouTube's controls.
f6b: Settings apply to running subtitles as soon as you save.

s3Text: Open a YouTube video and click Titl → Start subtitles. The first start prepares for about 12 seconds, then plays with subtitles.
s3a: Don't see Titl in the toolbar? Click the puzzle-piece icon and pin it.
s3b: Titl recognises the spoken language by itself. If it picks a similar one, for example Croatian instead of Serbian, choose the right one in Options → Spoken language.
s3c: A muted copy of the video plays a few seconds ahead in a collapsed Titl tab group, so each line is ready on time. Leave it open; it closes when you stop subtitles. Live streams have no copy, so their subtitles come 3–5 seconds late.
optText: Pick a language in Options → Translate to, and Chrome translates each line on your computer. For better translation on a powerful computer (16 GB of memory or more), set up a free AI model once with the step-by-step guide, then choose Options → Translator → Local LLM.
installNote: Works best on a recent Mac or a PC with an NVIDIA graphics card. Other computers work too, just a little slower. Needs 0.5–1.6 GB of free disk space. Detailed install guide
q8: How do I get subtitles on a YouTube video that has none?
a8: Install Titl and its helper, open the video and click Titl → Start subtitles. Titl makes the subtitles from the sound, so the video doesn't need captions. To read them in another language, choose one in Options → Translate to.
q1: Does my audio leave my computer?
a1: No. Titl recognises speech on your own computer, so the audio is never sent over the internet, not to us and not to anyone else. Translation also happens on your computer. See the privacy policy.
q2: Why does a muted tab open?
a2: To show subtitles on time, Titl plays a silent copy of the video a few seconds ahead. It's tucked away in a collapsed grey Titl tab group and closes when you stop.
a3: About 100 spoken languages. Translation goes into about 36 languages with Chrome's built-in translator (Chrome 138 or newer).
a6: Turn it on in Options → Translate to. Chrome translates each line right on your computer, and nothing is sent to a translation service. The language downloads once. Lines are translated a few seconds before they appear, so there's no delay. You can show the original above the translation, or blur the translation and reveal it with V.
q7: Can the translation be even better?
a7: Yes, on a powerful computer. Titl can translate with a free AI model, such as Google's Gemma, running on your own computer. It reads the lines around each sentence, so sentences split across lines come out right and names stay the same throughout. Nothing leaves your computer. It needs about 7 GB of disk space and 12 GB of memory. Set it up once with the step-by-step guide, then choose Options → Translator → Local LLM.
a9: Yes. Titl runs Whisper, OpenAI's open speech-recognition model, on your own computer with whisper.cpp. By default it uses the large-v3-turbo model on a Mac or a Windows PC with an NVIDIA graphics card, and the lighter small model on other computers.
q4: Do I need a powerful computer?
a4: No. On computers without a strong graphics card, Titl uses a lighter model that still keeps up with the video. At most, you'll wait a few extra seconds before the video starts.
a5: Nothing. Titl is free and MIT-licensed. If it helps you, support Titl on GitHub and/or on Ko-fi.
